claim: The Second Circuit places the burden on the defendant, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, and D.C. Circuits place it on the plaintiff.
evidence: The Second Circuit places the burden on the defendant: ... 'Since qualified immunity is an affirmative defense, the defendants bear the burden of showing that the challenged act was objectively reasonable in light of the law existing at that time.' ... The Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, and D.C. Circuits all likewise place the burden on the plaintiff: ... 'Sixth Circuit: ... the plaintiff bears the burden of showing that a defendant is not entitled to qualified immunity.'
excerpt:
Based on my review, the Fifth Circuit’s framework appears to be the majority rule. The Sixth, Seventh, Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh, and D.C. Circuits all likewise place the burden on the plaintiff:

Lias, 21 F.4th 74 (3d Cir. 2021) (“[T]he officer bears the burden of establishing his entitlement to qualified immunity….”). And in others, it places the burden on the plaintiff. See, e.g., Lozano v.
